adults.title: I See You: Looking at People the Way the Savior Does
adults.big_idea: Jesus Christ sees every person, including us, as a beloved child of God, and when we pray to see others as He does, love and service follow.
adults.objective: Learners will name one person who may feel unseen, plan a simple way to acknowledge that person this week, and feel more surely that the Savior sees them too.
prepare: Read President Chibota’s talk, marking paragraphs 1–8 and 10–14.
Bring a small slip of paper and a pencil for each person.
Write on the board: Who was overlooked? What did the one who stopped see? What did he do?
Pray by name for the people you will teach, asking to see them as Heavenly Father does.

segments.name: A greeting that means more than hello
steps: After the prayer, tell the class that President Chibota, the Primary General President, began her talk with the southern African greeting sawubona, which means “I see you.” Read her explanation in paragraph 1 (first key quote).
Ask the first question below. Give ten seconds of silence, then let people turn to a neighbor for one minute before two or three share with the class.
State the purpose of the lesson in one sentence: today we will learn from the Savior how to see people, and how He sees us.
questions: When has someone noticed you at a time you felt invisible? What did that person actually do?

segments.name: How the Savior saw people
steps: Divide into three groups (or three pairs). Assign Mark 10:21, John 5:2–9 and Luke 10:30–35, one to each.
Give four minutes to read and answer the three questions on the board.

Have each group report in one minute. As they do, read what President Chibota said about each account from paragraphs 2–4. Point out that she said the Savior loved the rich young man even though he later walked away sorrowing.
Read the second key quote aloud. Then share President Farnes’s words from this conference (aligned quote) and ask the question below.
questions: President Chibota said that where others saw labels, the Savior saw beloved sons and daughters of God. What gets in the way of our seeing people like that on an ordinary day?

segments.name: It can begin with a name
steps: Ask someone to read paragraphs 5–6, the account of the school janitor who thanked President Chibota and her husband for their daughter. She greeted him, knew his name, and helped him clean up after lunch.
Read the last sentence of paragraph 4: helping others feel seen often begins with something as simple as learning their name.
Hand out the slips of paper. Invite everyone to write silently the answer to the first question below. No one will be asked to share what they write.
Invite one or two to answer the second question aloud.
questions: Who do I pass every week, at church, at work or on my street, whose name I do not know or have forgotten?
Why does being called by name matter so much to us?

segments.name: Above every label
steps: Explain that President Chibota turned the lesson toward ourselves: seeing others as children of God also changes how we see ourselves.
Read paragraphs 11–13 together. Note what President Oaks told her when he extended her calling, and that it eased her feelings of inadequacy.
Ask learners to turn their slip over and write, for their eyes only, one label they carry that weighs on them. Then read the third key quote slowly.
Read Romans 4:17 and paragraph 9. Have learners write the three eternal truths from her invitation under their label: Child of God. Child of the covenant. Disciple of Jesus Christ.
Discuss the question below in pairs, then hear from one or two.
questions: How would this week be different if you believed, all the way down, that God’s view of you is more complete and more hopeful than your own?

segments.name: Choose, pray and act
steps: Read President Chibota’s three invitations for this week (see invitations). Ask each person to circle the name on the slip, or choose one of the other two invitations, and decide when they will act.

Share the promises she attached: when we ask Heavenly Father to help us see others, He guides us to those who feel unseen, and hearts change, relationships deepen, and faith grows. Read President Kimball’s words that she quoted (aligned quote).
Check for understanding: ask two people to finish this sentence aloud: This week I will see someone by…
Bear brief testimony that the Savior knows each person in the room by name. Tell the class you will begin next week by asking whose name they learned and what happened.
Follow up next week: open with that question and let two or three report before the new lesson.

key_quotes.text: It is an acknowledgment of another person’s worth and humanity. It communicates, “I recognize you. I respect you. You matter.”
Where others saw labels, He saw beloved sons and daughters of God.
Whatever labels may weigh heavily upon you today, Jesus Christ can raise you above them. His grace is sufficient to lift you above every label and limitation.
When we see others through the Savior’s eyes, love and service naturally follow.

scriptures.use: Group 1 reads it and reports how the Savior looked at the rich young man before asking something hard of him.
Group 2 reads it and reports who had been passed by at the pool of Bethesda and what the Savior did after He saw him.
Group 3 reads it and lists each thing the good Samaritan did once he chose to see the wounded man.
Read the end of the verse with paragraph 9 in the fourth segment; ask what it means that the Savior sees who we can become.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Farnes
aligned_quotes.text: To Jesus, these people were not interrupting His mission. They were His mission.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball
aligned_quotes.text: God does notice us, and … it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.

invitations.text: This week, I invite you to: Learn the name of someone who may feel unseen.
Pray to see others as Heavenly Father sees them.
Replace worldly labels with these eternal truths: Child of God. Child of the covenant. Disciple of Jesus Christ.

takeaways: The Savior sees beloved sons and daughters of God where others see labels.
Helping someone feel seen can begin with learning a name.
Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ see me, know my name, and see who I can become.
act: Learn the name of the person you wrote on your slip, and use it the next time you meet.
Each morning this week, pray to see the people you will meet as Heavenly Father sees them, then act on the first simple prompting to include someone.
When a heavy label comes to mind, say the three eternal truths to yourself: child of God, child of the covenant, disciple of Jesus Christ.
Greet one person at church next Sunday whom you have never spoken with.
music: I Am a Child of God
adapt: At home with two or three adults: skip the groups, read John 5:2–9 together, and spend the extra time on the slips of paper and the pair question about labels.
Large class: keep people in their rows and assign the three passages by section of the room; take one report per passage.
Only 15 minutes: do the opening question, John 5:2–9, the janitor account and the closing invitations.

youth.title: Seen: Names, Labels and Who You Really Are
youth.big_idea: Jesus Christ sees past every label to a child of God, and He asks us to see others, and ourselves, the same way.
youth.objective: Youth will explain how the Savior saw people others walked past, replace one label with an eternal truth, and choose one person whose name they will learn this week.
prepare: Read President Chibota’s talk, especially paragraphs 1–6 and 10–14.
Bring a half sheet of paper and a pen for each person, and something to write on the board with.
Ask the youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app open.
Write the three team questions on the board before class: Who was overlooked? What did Jesus or the Samaritan see? What did he do next?

segments.name: Sixty-second name challenge
steps: As soon as the prayer ends, hand out paper. Say: you have sixty seconds. Write the first names of adults you see every week who are not your teachers, leaders or family: a bus driver, a custodian, someone who serves lunch, a neighbor, a store clerk. Only names count, not job titles.
Time it. Ask for the highest count and congratulate the winner. Then ask who had a job in mind but no name to write. Most hands will go up, including yours.
Say: hold on to that blank. We will come back to it.

segments.name: Your daughter sees me
steps: Tell them President Chibota, the Primary General President, taught about the southern African greeting sawubona, which means “I see you.” Have someone read paragraph 1.
Have another youth read paragraphs 5–6, about the school janitor. Let the janitor’s words land: “Very few students know my name. Your daughter sees me.”
Ask the questions below. Take quick answers; do not correct.
questions: The daughter did three things: greeted him, knew his name, helped him clean up after lunch. Which of those is hardest at your school, and why?
Who at school is easy to walk past?

segments.name: Three teams, three people Jesus saw
steps: Make three teams. Assign Mark 10:21, John 5:2–9 and Luke 10:30–35.

Each team has four minutes to read and prepare a thirty-second report answering the three questions on the board. Creative reports are welcome: a quick sketch on the board, a news headline, or a ten-second freeze-frame acting it out.

Hear the reports. After each, read President Chibota’s sentence about that account from paragraphs 2–4. Point out that the man at the pool had been ill 38 years and that she said others had walked past him for years.
Read the first key quote together and ask the question below.
questions: In each account, what did the one who stopped notice that everyone else missed?

segments.name: Labels on the board
steps: Ask the class to call out labels people get at school or online, never a real person’s name, only the labels: popular, weird, smart, benchwarmer, new kid. Write them all over the board for one minute.
Ask the first question below. Then have someone read paragraphs 10–11 and the second key quote.
Tell them President Chibota said she has sometimes viewed herself through labels too. Read what President Oaks told her in paragraph 12, and then paragraph 14.
Invite a youth to come up, erase or cross out the labels, and write her three eternal truths large in the middle: Child of God. Child of the covenant. Disciple of Jesus Christ.
Give one minute of silent writing on the back of their paper: one label I am tired of carrying, and the truth I will put in its place. This stays private.
questions: Which of these labels would still be true about a person in five years? Which were true before they were born?
President Chibota said our identity is not something we achieve but something we inherit. Why is that good news on a bad day?

segments.name: What if I am the one who feels unseen?
steps: Say plainly that some weeks every one of us feels like the person nobody notices. Read paragraph 22 slowly (third key quote).
Read Sister Muñoz Spannaus’s words from this conference (aligned quote).
Invite anyone who wishes to answer the question below. Allow silence. Share a brief testimony of your own that the Savior knows them by name.
questions: When have you felt that Heavenly Father knew what was going on in your life?

segments.name: This week’s challenge
steps: Read President Chibota’s three invitations (see invitations). Go back to the blank from the name challenge: have each youth write one person whose name they will learn before next Sunday.
Have them take out their phones and type the three eternal truths into a note or reminder they will see each morning, along with the words pray to see.
Share her promise from her own experience with a coworker: when we ask Heavenly Father to help us see others, He guides us to those who feel unseen. Read President Farnes’s words (aligned quote).
Check for understanding: ask two youth to say in one sentence what sawubona means and whom they will say it to, in their own way, this week.
Follow up next week: start class with a one-minute report. Ask whose name they learned and what the person’s reaction was. Share your own first.

key_quotes.text: Where others saw labels, He saw beloved sons and daughters of God.
Our identity is not something we achieve; it is something we inherit as beloved sons and daughters of God.
I see you. More important, your Heavenly Father sees you. Your Savior, Jesus Christ, sees you. They know your name, your circumstances, your gifts, and your divine potential.
That eternal identity does not change when circumstances change, when we make mistakes, or when others misunderstand us.

scriptures.use: Team 1 reads it and reports what the Savior felt for the rich young man as He looked at him.
Team 2 reads it and reports who had been overlooked at the pool of Bethesda and what the Savior did.
Team 3 reads it and reports who walked past, who stopped, and everything the Samaritan did to help.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Sister Muñoz Spannaus
aligned_quotes.text: knowing everything about you does not make Him love you less

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Farnes
aligned_quotes.text: let us pray every day for eyes to see the divine appointments God places before us!

invitations.text: This week, I invite you to: Learn the name of someone who may feel unseen.
Pray to see others as Heavenly Father sees them.
Replace worldly labels with these eternal truths: Child of God. Child of the covenant. Disciple of Jesus Christ.

takeaways: Jesus sees a child of God where other people see a label.
My identity as a child of God is inherited, not earned, and it does not change when I make mistakes.
Learning one name can help someone feel seen.
act: Learn the name of one person at school or in your neighborhood who may feel unseen, and greet that person by name at least twice this week.
Before school each day, pray to see others as Heavenly Father sees them, and follow one prompting to include someone.
When a label about yourself or someone else comes to mind, replace it with child of God.
Thank a custodian, bus driver or lunch worker by name.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: do the name challenge together as a family list, read John 5:2–9 only, and spend more time on the private writing about labels.
Large class: run six teams, two per passage, and let the class vote on the clearest thirty-second report.
No phones in class: have youth write the three eternal truths on their paper and put it where they will see it each morning.

children.title: Jesus Sees Me, and I Can See Others
children.big_idea: Heavenly Father and Jesus see me and know my name, and I can help others feel seen by being kind and learning their names.
children.objective: Children will say that they are children of God whom Jesus sees and loves, and will choose one person to greet kindly by name this week.
prepare: Read paragraphs 1–6 and 22 of President Chibota’s talk and John 5:2–9.
Bring a soft ball, a small blanket or towel, and a flashlight.
Bring paper and crayons for each child.
Learn each child’s name before class so you can greet every one at the door.

segments.name: I see you
steps: Greet each child by name as they come in. After the prayer, sit in a circle on the floor.

Tell the children that President Chibota, who leads the Primary for the whole Church, taught about a greeting from southern Africa. It is sawubona, and it means “I see you.” Say the word together two times.
Roll the ball to a child and say: I see you, and then the child’s name. That child rolls it to someone else and says the same. Keep going until every child has been named.
Ask the question below.
questions: How does it feel when someone knows your name and says hello to you?

segments.name: Sing about it
steps: Stand up and stretch. Sing I Am a Child of God together.
Teach the short truth for today with actions: point to yourself for I am a child of God, then open your hands toward the others for So are you. Say it together three times, getting quieter each time.

segments.name: Jesus saw the man by the pool
steps: Lay the blanket on the floor. Tell the account from John 5:2–9 in simple words: a man lay by a pool called Bethesda. He had been sick for 38 years. President Chibota said many people had walked past him for years.
Choose a child to lie on the blanket. Have the other children walk past slowly, looking the other way. Then ask them to freeze.
Say: then Jesus came. He did not walk past. He saw the man. He talked with him and healed him. Have the child stand up, pick up the blanket and walk. Let everyone cheer quietly.
Repeat with a new child on the blanket if time allows. Ask the questions below.
questions: What did Jesus do that the other people did not do?
Does Jesus see you? How do you know?

segments.name: The flashlight helps us see
steps: Hold up the flashlight. Ask a child to point it at something small in the room that is easy to miss, such as a doorknob or a corner of the ceiling. Let two or three children take a turn.
Explain: the flashlight helps us notice things we were not looking at. When we pray, Heavenly Father helps us notice people who need a friend.
Shine the light gently on the floor in front of each child in turn, never in eyes, and say: Heavenly Father sees you. You are a child of God. Have the class repeat the second sentence each time.
Tell them President Chibota asked us to pray to see others the way Heavenly Father sees them.
questions: Who might need a friend to notice them at school or at church?

segments.name: The girl who knew his name
steps: Tell this true account from the talk: President Chibota’s daughter went to a school where a janitor worked to keep it clean. She said hello to him, she knew his name, and she even helped him clean up after lunch. One day the janitor, with tears in his eyes, thanked her parents. He told them, “Very few students know my name. Your daughter sees me.”
Ask the first question below.

Practice. Have the children stand and walk around the room. When you clap, each child stops, faces the nearest person, smiles and says hello with that person’s name. Clap four or five times so they greet different children. Help anyone who does not know a name to ask kindly: What is your name?
questions: What three kind things did the daughter do?
Who helps at your school or at church whose name you could learn?

segments.name: Draw someone I will see
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw one person they will say hello to by name this week: a child in their class, a neighbor, a helper at school or at church.
As they draw, go to each child and ask who it is and what they will say. Write the person’s name on the paper if they know it, or write Learn the name if they do not.
Invite two or three children to hold up their pictures and tell the class about them.

segments.name: Remember and close
steps: Sing or say the line from the Primary song that President Chibota quoted: “Jesus said love ev’ryone; treat them kindly too.”
Say the truth with actions one more time: I am a child of God. So are you.
Bear a short testimony that Heavenly Father and Jesus know each child’s name. Invite the children to take their picture home and tell their family whom they will greet.
Follow up next week: as you greet each child at the door, ask whom they said hello to and whether they learned a new name.

key_quotes.text: Very few students know my name. Your daughter sees me.
your Heavenly Father sees you. Your Savior, Jesus Christ, sees you. They know your name
Jesus said love ev’ryone; treat them kindly too.

scriptures.use: Tell the account in simple words while the children act it out with the blanket; older children can read verses 8–9 aloud.
If you have extra time, tell the story of the good Samaritan and ask who stopped to help the hurt man.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

invitations.text: This week, I invite you to: Learn the name of someone who may feel unseen.
Pray to see others as Heavenly Father sees them.

takeaways: I am a child of God, and so is everyone I meet.
Heavenly Father and Jesus see me and know my name.
I can help others feel seen by saying hello and learning their names.
act: Say hello by name to the person in your drawing.
Learn the name of one helper at school or at church and say thank you.
When you pray this week, ask Heavenly Father to help you notice someone who needs a friend.
music: I Am a Child of God

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep each part short and moving. Repeat the ball game and the blanket story so every child has a turn, and say I am a child of God, so are you with actions after every activity. Skip the questions that need long answers; instead ask children to show you a kind hello. Ask an older child or another adult to help with names during the clapping game and to write on the drawings.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have a child read John 5:5–9 aloud before acting it out, and let an older child lead the clapping game. Ask a harder question: why do we sometimes walk past people without noticing them, and what could help us stop? Invite them to write on their drawing one thing, besides saying hello, that they could do for that person, as President Chibota’s daughter did when she helped clean up after lunch.
